“I will now move on to the more emotional part of my story. I will describe the events whose powerful effect on my feelings changed me from what I was into what I am today.

“Spring came quickly. The weather grew pleasant and the skies clear. I was amazed that the landscape, once so bare and gloomy, now bloomed with beautiful flowers and greenery. Countless lovely scents and sights delighted my senses and made me feel renewed.

“One day, during one of the cottage family’s regular breaks from work, the old man played his guitar while his children listened. I noticed that Felix looked more sorrowful than words could express. He sighed often. Once his father stopped playing, and from his manner I guessed he was asking what troubled his son. Felix answered cheerfully. The old man was about to resume his music when someone knocked at the door.

“The visitor was a woman on horseback, with a countryman accompanying her as a guide. She wore dark clothes and a thick black veil. Agatha asked her something, but she answered only by saying Felix’s name in a sweet voice. Her voice was musical, though unlike either of my friends’ voices. Hearing his name, Felix hurried toward her. When she saw him, she lifted her veil, revealing a face of angelic beauty and expression. Her glossy black hair was intricately braided. Her dark eyes were lively yet gentle, her features beautifully balanced, and her skin wonderfully fair, with a lovely pink color in each cheek.

“Felix seemed overwhelmed with delight at the sight of her. Every trace of sadness left his face, which instantly showed a joy so intense I could scarcely have believed it possible. His eyes shone and his cheeks flushed with pleasure. At that moment, I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. Her feelings seemed different. Wiping a few tears from her lovely eyes, she offered Felix her hand. He kissed it joyfully and called her, as nearly as I could make out, his sweet Arabian. She seemed not to understand him, but she smiled. He helped her down from her horse, sent her guide away, and led her into the cottage. After he and his father spoke for a little while, the young stranger knelt at the old man’s feet and tried to kiss his hand. Instead, he helped her up and embraced her warmly.

“I soon realized that although the stranger spoke clearly and seemed to have a language of her own, the cottage family could not understand her, nor could she understand them.

“Then listen, you!” Monks replied. “When his father fell ill in Rome, his wife—my mother—went to him from Paris and took me along. They had been separated for a long time. For all I know, she went to protect his property, since she had little affection for him, and he had little for her. He did not recognize us. He had lost consciousness and slept until the next day, when he died. In his desk were two documents, both dated the night his illness began, addressed to you.” He turned to Mr. Brownlow. “They came with a short note for you. The outside of the package said it must not be sent until after his death. One document was a letter to that girl Agnes; the other was a will.”

“What did the letter say?” Mr. Brownlow asked.

“The letter? A sheet covered with writing in one direction and then across it again: a remorseful confession and prayers for God to help her. He had convinced the girl that some secret, which he would explain one day, prevented him from marrying her just then. She had patiently trusted him until she trusted too far and lost what no one could restore. Her child was due in a few months. He told her everything he had intended to do, if he lived, to conceal her disgrace. If he died, he begged her not to curse his memory or believe that she or their child would be punished for their sin, because the blame was entirely his. He reminded her of the day he gave her the little locket and the ring engraved with her first name, with a space left for the surname he hoped to give her someday. He begged her to keep it and wear it close to her heart, as before. Then he rambled wildly, repeating the same words again and again, as though he had lost his mind. I believe he had.”

“The will,” said Mr. Brownlow, while Oliver’s tears flowed freely.

Monks said nothing.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow continued, answering for him, “expressed the same feelings as the letter. He described the suffering his wife had caused him. He spoke of your rebellious nature, your wickedness and malice, and the bad passions you developed so young—you, his only son, who had been taught to hate him. He left you and your mother eight hundred pounds a year each. Most of his property he divided equally between Agnes Fleming and their child, provided the child was born alive and lived to adulthood.

“Come on, Tom,” I said. “You could at least tell me. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, I don’t know. But he has to have one. All noblemen do.”

That was typical of him. If he didn’t feel like explaining something, he simply wouldn’t. You could question him for a week and get nowhere.

Now that he had settled all the business of the coat of arms, he moved on to the rest of that work: composing a sorrowful inscription. Jim needed one, he said, like every other prisoner. He thought up several, wrote them on a sheet of paper, and read them aloud:

“Here a prisoner’s heart burst.”

“Here a poor prisoner, abandoned by his friends and the world, wasted his sorrowful life away.”

“Here a lonely heart broke, and an exhausted spirit found rest after thirty-seven years imprisoned alone.”

“Here, without home or friends, a noble stranger, the illegitimate son of Louis XIV, died after thirty-seven years of bitter imprisonment.”

Tom’s voice shook as he read them, and he nearly burst into tears. When he finished, he couldn’t decide which Jim should scratch on the wall, because they were all so good. Finally, he decided to let him carve every one of them. Jim said scratching all that nonsense into the logs with a nail would take a year, and besides, he didn’t know how to write letters. Tom said he would draw their outlines, so Jim would only have to follow the marks. A little later, he said:

“Actually, the logs won’t do. Dungeons don’t have log walls. We need to carve the inscriptions into stone. We’ll bring in a rock.”

Jim said stone was worse than wood. Carving all those words into a rock would take so terribly long that he would never escape. But Tom said he would allow me to help him. Then he checked how Jim and I were getting on with the pens. It was painfully slow, difficult, boring work. The sores on my hands had no chance to heal, and we hardly seemed to be making any progress. So Tom said:

“I know what to do. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the sorrowful inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that same stone.
